_comment: Muscle/bone knowledge base for the interactive 3D anatomy explorer. Each entry: match[] = lowercase substrings tested against the GLB node name-path (FIRST match wins, so order specific->general). name = clean display label. function = plain-English what-it-does. massage = Mike's first-person note (deep-tissue / medical massage, Tarpon Springs). Resolver falls back to fallbackByTissue when nothing matches.

entries.name: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM)
entries.function: The rope-like muscle on the side of your neck that turns and tilts your head and helps you nod.
entries.massage: When your SCM is tight it can drive headaches behind the eye and that 'crick' when you check your blind spot. I release it gently by hand — it's one of the most overlooked headache muscles.

entries.name: Scalene muscles
entries.function: Deep neck muscles that flex and side-bend the neck and lift the upper ribs when you breathe hard.
entries.massage: Tight scalenes can pinch the nerves to your arm and cause tingling in the hand. I work them carefully — this is often the real source of 'shoulder' numbness.

entries.name: Splenius (neck)
entries.function: Straps along the back of the neck that extend the head and rotate it to the same side.
entries.massage: These get loaded from screen-and-phone posture. Loosening them gives back that easy range of motion when you turn your head.

entries.name: Levator scapulae
entries.function: Runs from the neck to the shoulder blade and shrugs/lifts the scapula — it's the muscle you rub when you're stressed.
entries.massage: Classic 'I carry my stress in my shoulders' muscle. I find the knot at the corner of the shoulder blade and work it until the shoulder drops.

entries.name: Trapezius
entries.function: The big diamond across the upper back and neck — it shrugs, steadies, and rotates the shoulder blades.
entries.massage: Upper traps are where desk tension piles up. I work the whole sheet so your shoulders sit down where they belong instead of up by your ears.

entries.name: Rhomboids
entries.function: Between the spine and shoulder blade, they pull the blades together and back for upright posture.
entries.massage: Rounded-forward posture leaves these long and aching between the shoulder blades. Targeted work here is a big part of fixing desk hunch.

entries.name: Latissimus dorsi
entries.function: The broad 'wing' muscle of the back that pulls the arm down and back and supports the spine.
entries.massage: Tight lats round the shoulders and limit overhead reach. I trace it from the armpit down — climbers, swimmers and gym folks always feel this one.

entries.name: Serratus anterior
entries.function: Finger-like muscle on the ribs that wraps to the shoulder blade and lets you reach and push.
entries.massage: Often missed and often the reason a shoulder won't move freely. Releasing it can unlock a stubborn shoulder fast.

entries.name: Supraspinatus (rotator cuff)
entries.function: Rotator-cuff muscle on top of the shoulder blade that starts lifting the arm out to the side.
entries.massage: The most commonly impinged cuff muscle. I work it to take pressure off that painful arc when you raise your arm.

entries.name: Infraspinatus (rotator cuff)
entries.function: Rotator-cuff muscle on the back of the shoulder blade that rotates the arm outward.
entries.massage: A huge source of referred pain down the arm. Trigger points here fool people into thinking it's elbow or wrist pain.

entries.name: Subscapularis (rotator cuff)
entries.function: Rotator-cuff muscle on the front of the shoulder blade that rotates the arm inward.
entries.massage: Hard to reach and often the hidden culprit in frozen shoulder. I know how to access it safely to restore rotation.

entries.name: Teres minor (rotator cuff)
entries.function: Small rotator-cuff muscle that helps rotate the arm outward and stabilize the shoulder.
entries.massage: Part of the cuff team I always check when a shoulder aches at the back — small muscle, big relief when it lets go.

entries.name: Teres major
entries.function: Works with the lat to pull the arm down and in toward the body.
entries.massage: Tucked along the edge of the shoulder blade. Loosening it helps the whole shoulder glide instead of grind.

entries.name: Deltoid
entries.function: The cap of the shoulder — its three parts raise the arm forward, out to the side, and back.
entries.massage: Takes a beating from lifting and overhead work. I work all three heads so the shoulder moves clean in every direction.

entries.name: Pectoralis major
entries.function: The big chest muscle that pulls the arm across the body and powers pushing.
entries.massage: Tight chest = rounded shoulders. Opening the pecs is half of fixing the desk-and-phone posture I see every day.

entries.name: Pectoralis minor
entries.function: Small deep chest muscle that tips the shoulder blade forward; tightness rounds the shoulders.
entries.massage: It can compress the nerves and vessels to the arm. Releasing it relieves arm tingling and lets the shoulders settle back.

entries.name: Subclavius
entries.function: Small muscle under the collarbone that steadies it during arm movement.
entries.massage: Tiny but tender — I check it when the front of the shoulder feels jammed.

entries.name: Biceps brachii
entries.function: Front of the upper arm — bends the elbow and turns the palm up.
entries.massage: Curls and carrying tighten it. I work it with the forearm so the elbow stops aching.

entries.name: Brachialis / upper arm
entries.function: Deep elbow flexor under the biceps that does much of the heavy lifting when you bend your arm.
entries.massage: The 'workhorse' elbow bender. Often the real source of stubborn elbow pain people blame on tennis elbow.

entries.name: Triceps brachii
entries.function: Back of the upper arm — straightens the elbow.
entries.massage: Gets short from pressing and pushing. Loosening it restores a clean, full elbow extension.

entries.name: Brachioradialis
entries.function: Forearm muscle that bends the elbow, especially with the thumb up.
entries.massage: Grip-and-mouse tension lands here. Working it eases that ache along the top of the forearm.

entries.name: Pronator (forearm)
entries.function: Turns the forearm so the palm faces down.
entries.massage: Tight pronators can mimic carpal tunnel. I release them to take pressure off the nerve at the wrist.

entries.name: Forearm flexors
entries.function: Muscles on the palm side of the forearm that curl the wrist and fingers and power your grip.
entries.massage: Keyboard, phone and tool use overload these. This is ground zero for grip pain and a lot of so-called carpal tunnel.

entries.name: Forearm extensors
entries.function: Back-of-forearm muscles that straighten the wrist and fingers.
entries.massage: Tennis-elbow territory. Releasing them at the elbow and along the forearm calms that outer-elbow burn.

entries.name: Palmaris longus
entries.function: Small forearm muscle that helps tense the palm and assist wrist flexion.
entries.massage: Minor player, but I include it when I'm clearing tight, grippy forearms.

entries.name: Supinator
entries.function: Turns the forearm so the palm faces up.
entries.massage: I work it alongside the extensors when the outer elbow won't settle down.

entries.name: Rectus abdominis
entries.function: The 'six-pack' — flexes the trunk forward and supports the core.
entries.massage: Tight abs can pull you into a slump and aggravate low-back pain. Gentle abdominal work is part of unwinding posture.

entries.name: Abdominal obliques
entries.function: Side-of-waist muscles that twist and side-bend the trunk and brace the core.
entries.massage: Key for rotation and a stable low back. I address them when twisting motions or breathing feel restricted.

entries.name: Transverse abdominis
entries.function: Deep corset muscle that wraps the abdomen and stabilizes the spine.
entries.massage: Your built-in back brace. Supporting it is part of long-term low-back relief.

entries.name: Quadratus lumborum (QL)
entries.function: Deep low-back muscle that hikes the hip and side-bends the spine.
entries.massage: One of the top hidden causes of nagging low-back pain. When I find a tight QL, releasing it is often the 'aha' moment.

entries.name: Pyramidalis
entries.function: Small muscle low in the abdomen that tenses the midline.
entries.massage: Minor, but I keep it in mind when the lower abdomen feels guarded.

entries.name: Erector spinae
entries.function: The long columns running either side of the spine that hold you upright and extend and rotate the back.
entries.massage: These work all day to keep you vertical. Deep, slow work along them is the heart of back-pain relief.

entries.name: Deep spinal muscles
entries.function: Short deep muscles between the vertebrae that fine-tune posture and stabilize each segment of the spine.
entries.massage: The deepest layer of back support. Reaching them takes skill — it's where stubborn segmental stiffness lives.

entries.name: Intercostal muscles
entries.function: Muscles between the ribs that move the rib cage as you breathe.
entries.massage: Tight intercostals make breaths feel shallow and the mid-back stiff. Freeing them helps you breathe deeper.

entries.name: Diaphragm
entries.function: The dome under the lungs — your main breathing muscle.
entries.massage: Stress lives in the breath. Gentle work around the lower ribs helps the diaphragm move freely again.

entries.name: Psoas / iliopsoas
entries.function: Deep hip flexor running from the lower spine to the thigh — it lifts the knee and is central to posture.
entries.massage: Sitting all day shortens the psoas and tugs on the low back. Carefully releasing it is one of the biggest wins for low-back and hip pain.

entries.name: Iliacus
entries.function: Sits inside the pelvis and joins the psoas to flex the hip.
entries.massage: Part of the deep hip-flexor team I address when the front of the hip feels locked from sitting.

entries.name: Piriformis
entries.function: Deep glute muscle that rotates the hip outward; it sits right over the sciatic nerve.
entries.massage: The famous sciatica mimic. When it's tight it can press the sciatic nerve and shoot pain down the leg — releasing it is often instant relief.

entries.name: Gluteus maximus
entries.function: The big, powerful glute that extends the hip and drives standing, climbing and lifting.
entries.massage: A weak, tight glute throws the whole low back and hip off. Deep work here restores power and takes load off the spine.

entries.name: Gluteus medius / minimus
entries.function: Side-hip muscles that steady the pelvis when you walk and lift the leg out to the side.
entries.massage: Trigger points here refer pain into the low back and down the leg. They're a frequent hidden source of 'hip' pain.

entries.name: Tensor fasciae latae (TFL)
entries.function: Small muscle at the front of the hip that tightens the IT band and helps flex and rotate the hip.
entries.massage: A tight TFL/IT band tugs on the knee and outer thigh. Runners and cyclists feel a real difference when I free it.

entries.name: Deep hip rotators
entries.function: Small deep muscles around the hip socket that rotate the thigh and stabilize the joint.
entries.massage: The deep six. They're part of the sciatica-and-hip picture I check whenever the buttock aches deep.

entries.name: Gracilis
entries.function: Long slender inner-thigh muscle that pulls the leg inward and helps bend the knee.
entries.massage: Inner-thigh tightness shows up here. I include it when the groin or inner knee feels strained.

entries.name: Adductors (inner thigh)
entries.function: Inner-thigh muscles that draw the legs together and stabilize the pelvis.
entries.massage: Groin strains and inner-thigh tightness live here. Careful, respectful work makes a big difference for athletes and walkers alike.

entries.name: Sartorius
entries.function: The long 'tailor's muscle' that crosses the thigh to flex and rotate the hip and bend the knee.
entries.massage: It runs corner to corner across the thigh; I follow it when the front of the hip and inner knee feel pulled.

entries.name: Rectus femoris (quadriceps)
entries.function: The quad muscle that crosses both the hip and knee — it straightens the knee and flexes the hip.
entries.massage: Sitting and squatting load it heavily. Releasing it eases front-of-knee and hip-flexor tightness.

entries.name: Quadriceps (vastus group)
entries.function: The big front-thigh muscles that straighten the knee and absorb load when you walk and stand.
entries.massage: Tight quads pull on the kneecap and tilt the pelvis. Deep work here helps knees track right and low backs relax.

entries.name: Hamstrings
entries.function: Back-of-thigh muscles that bend the knee and extend the hip.
entries.massage: Chronically tight hamstrings tilt the pelvis and feed low-back pain. Lengthening them is a core part of fixing posture.

entries.name: Gastrocnemius (calf)
entries.function: The big calf muscle that points the foot down and powers walking, running and jumping.
entries.massage: Tight calves change how you walk and stress the knee and heel. Calf work is key for plantar-fasciitis and foot pain.

entries.name: Soleus (deep calf)
entries.function: Deep calf muscle under the gastrocnemius that points the foot and steadies you when standing.
entries.massage: The deep calf that holds you upright all day. Releasing it relieves a lot of stubborn lower-leg and heel tension.

entries.name: Tibialis anterior (shin)
entries.function: Front-of-shin muscle that lifts the foot and toes as you walk.
entries.massage: Shin-splint territory. I work it for runners and anyone whose shins burn after walking.

entries.name: Fibularis / peroneals
entries.function: Outer-lower-leg muscles that turn the foot outward and stabilize the ankle.
entries.massage: Key for ankle stability. I address them after ankle sprains and for outer-shin tightness.

entries.name: Plantar fascia / foot
entries.function: The thick band along the sole that supports the arch of the foot.
entries.massage: Heel-pain central. Working the calf and the sole together is how I tackle stubborn plantar fasciitis.

entries.name: Masseter
entries.function: The main chewing muscle at the angle of the jaw.
entries.massage: Jaw clenchers and TMJ sufferers hold tons of tension here. Gentle release eases jaw ache and headaches.

entries.name: Temporalis
entries.function: Fan-shaped muscle at the temple that closes the jaw.
entries.massage: Tension headaches at the temples often start here. I work it lightly to calm jaw-driven headaches.

entries.name: Quadratus
entries.function: A flat 'four-sided' stabilizing muscle (the name marks several in the body).
entries.massage: I identify exactly which one and work it in context — stabilizers like this quietly drive a lot of pain.

entries.name: Fascia
entries.function: The connective-tissue webbing that wraps and links every muscle — it transmits force and can bind down when injured or inactive.
entries.massage: Fascia is the unsung hero of bodywork. Slow, sustained pressure (and cupping) rehydrates and unsticks it so muscles glide freely again.

entries.name: Spine (vertebrae)
entries.function: The stacked bones that protect the spinal cord and let you bend, twist and stay upright.
entries.massage: I never adjust bones — I free the muscles around the spine so each segment can move the way it's meant to.

entries.name: Scapula (shoulder blade)
entries.function: The flat shoulder-blade bone that anchors the shoulder and arm muscles.
entries.massage: So many shoulder problems are really about how the scapula glides. I work the muscles that move it to restore that glide.

entries.name: Clavicle (collarbone)
entries.function: The strut that connects the arm to the chest and keeps the shoulder set back.
entries.massage: A landmark I work around to release the chest and front-of-shoulder tension that rounds posture.

entries.name: Humerus
entries.function: The upper-arm bone, anchor for the shoulder and elbow muscles.
entries.massage: I use it as a lever to find and release the arm and shoulder muscles attached along it.

entries.name: Forearm bones (radius & ulna)
entries.function: The two forearm bones that let your wrist turn and your hand position.
entries.massage: I trace the muscles along them to clear grip and wrist tension.

entries.name: Pelvis
entries.function: The bony bowl that links the spine to the legs and anchors the core and hip muscles.
entries.massage: The crossroads of the body. So much low-back and hip pain comes down to the muscles balancing the pelvis.

entries.name: Femur (thigh bone)
entries.function: The long thigh bone — the body's largest, anchoring the hip and knee muscles.
entries.massage: I work the powerful muscles wrapping it to settle hip and knee complaints.

entries.name: Patella (kneecap)
entries.function: The kneecap — it improves the leverage of the quadriceps over the knee.
entries.massage: How the kneecap tracks depends on quad and IT-band balance. I address those to ease front-of-knee pain.

entries.name: Lower-leg bones (tibia & fibula)
entries.function: The shin and outer lower-leg bones that bear your weight and anchor the calf and shin muscles.
entries.massage: Landmarks for clearing shin, calf and ankle tension.

entries.name: Foot & ankle bones
entries.function: The many small bones that form the flexible, weight-bearing arches of the foot.
entries.massage: Feet take a pounding. Working the muscles and fascia that move these bones relieves heel and arch pain.

entries.name: Rib cage
entries.function: The bony cage that protects the heart and lungs and moves with every breath.
entries.massage: I free the muscles between and around the ribs so breathing feels open and the mid-back loosens.

entries.name: Skull & jaw
entries.function: The bones of the head and jaw that protect the brain and let you chew and speak.
entries.massage: I focus on the jaw and the base of the skull — releasing those muscles calms tension headaches and TMJ.

entries.name: Cartilage
entries.function: Smooth, cushioning connective tissue that lets joints glide and absorbs shock.
entries.massage: I don't work cartilage directly — I keep the surrounding muscles balanced so your joints are loaded evenly and comfortably.

entries.name: Sciatic nerve
entries.function: The body's largest nerve — it runs from the low back through the buttock and down the back of the leg.
entries.massage: When the piriformis or deep glutes clamp down on this nerve, you get that shooting leg pain. Releasing those muscles is how I take the pressure off it.

entries.name: Median nerve
entries.function: Runs down the arm into the hand; it's the nerve squeezed in carpal tunnel syndrome.
entries.massage: Tight forearm and pronator muscles can compress this nerve. Freeing them often eases the hand tingling people blame purely on the wrist.

entries.name: Ulnar nerve
entries.function: The 'funny bone' nerve — runs to the ring and little fingers.
entries.massage: I check the muscles around the elbow and inner forearm when those fingers tingle or go numb.

entries.name: Radial nerve
entries.function: Powers the muscles that straighten the wrist and fingers.
entries.massage: Tightness in the upper arm and forearm can irritate it; I work those to keep the wrist working freely.

entries.name: Femoral nerve
entries.function: Supplies the front of the thigh and the quadriceps.
entries.massage: Tight hip flexors can crowd this nerve. Releasing the psoas and front of the hip gives it room.

entries.name: Nerve plexus
entries.function: A web where spinal nerves bundle and branch out to the limb.
entries.massage: The neck, scalenes and chest can crowd these bundles. Opening that area relieves a lot of arm tingling and numbness.

entries.name: Nerve
entries.function: Part of the body's wiring — nerves carry signals between the brain, spinal cord, muscles and skin.
entries.massage: I never work nerves directly. I release the tight muscles and fascia that can crowd a nerve, which calms the tingling, numbness or shooting pain it causes.

entries.name: Aorta
entries.function: The body's main artery — it carries oxygen-rich blood straight out of the heart.
entries.massage: Shown here so you can see how the plumbing runs. I work muscle and fascia, never the vessels themselves.

entries.name: Carotid artery
entries.function: The large neck artery feeding the brain and head.
entries.massage: A landmark I stay clear of — neck work is always done with care around the vessels.

entries.name: Femoral artery
entries.function: The main artery supplying the leg, running through the front of the hip.
entries.massage: Another reason hip work is done thoughtfully — I work around the vessels, on the muscles.

entries.name: Artery
entries.function: Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood away from the heart to the muscles and organs.
entries.massage: Good circulation is half of why massage feels so good — relaxed muscles let blood move freely. I work the tissue, not the vessels.

entries.name: Major vein
entries.function: Large veins that return blood back toward the heart.
entries.massage: Shown for context. Easing muscle tension helps overall circulation and that 'lighter' feeling after a session.

entries.name: Vein
entries.function: Veins return oxygen-poor blood back to the heart.
entries.massage: Relaxed, well-worked muscle supports healthy venous return — part of why you feel less heavy and tense afterward.

muscle.name: Muscle
muscle.function: A muscle that moves or stabilizes part of your body.
muscle.massage: If this is an area that's bothering you, tell me where it hurts and I'll build the session around it.

bone.name: Bone
bone.function: Part of your skeletal frame — it gives shape, protects organs, and anchors muscles.
bone.massage: I work the muscles attached to this bone, never the bone itself, to restore easy movement.

nerve.name: Nerve
nerve.function: Part of the body's wiring, carrying signals to and from the muscles and skin.
nerve.massage: I never work nerves directly — I free the tight muscles that can crowd them, which calms tingling and referred pain.

artery.name: Artery
artery.function: Carries oxygen-rich blood away from the heart.
artery.massage: Shown for context. I work muscle and fascia, never the vessels — relaxed muscle helps circulation on its own.

vein.name: Vein
vein.function: Returns blood back toward the heart.
vein.massage: Shown for context. Easing muscle tension supports healthy circulation and that lighter feeling afterward.

other.name: Body structure
other.function: A structure in the body's soft-tissue and connective network.
other.massage: Point me to what's bothering you and I'll tailor the work to it.
